text.p: U.S. athletics officials reversed course on Tuesday and declared suspended runner Mary Slaney eligible for this week's national championships. But they remained undecided on whether they would comply with an IAAF order to prohibit her from running.

In sharp contrast to an earlier statement that USA Track and Field "would invalidate" Slaney's entry, federation spokesman Pete Cava said, "USA Track and Field considers Mary Slaney an eligible athlete."

Asked whether that meant the U.S. federation would permit Slaney to run in the championships in defiance of the IAAF order, Cava said, "Right now, I do not know. Maybe tomorrow (Wednesday) I will have an answer for you, but right now, I do not know. We are studying our options and procedures."
Cava said the decision to make Slaney "eligible" came after U.S. officials had consulted with counsel Peter Alkaly concerning the IAAF order.
Slaney's husband, Richard, was befuddled by the U.S. action.
"What does this mean?" he said from the couple's home in Eugene, Oregon. "Here it is Tuesday afternoon and we don't know what they're doing."

Slaney and fellow Americans Sandra Farmer-Patrick and Stephon Flenoy were suspended by the IAAF 10 days ago pending the outcome of U.S. hearings into drug tests last summer. In each case the athlete was found to have a higher than acceptable ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone. Under IAAF rules, any ratio above 6-1 is considered suspicious and an athlete is subject to suspension.

Slaney and Farmer-Patrick have denied taking any substance banned by the IAAF, but IAAF general secretary Istvan Gyulai, reached in Monte Carlo, said, "There is a very clear indication that this (Slaney) is a doping case."
Cava said a letter from the IAAF, which the U.S. federation received Tuesday, said the IAAF considered "Mary Slaney suspended" and "cannot compete nationally or internationally."
He said the world governing body also reminded U.S. officials of the so-called "contamination" rule whereby athletes can be suspended if they compete against ineligible participants.

Asked prior to Cava's second statement what would happen if the U.S. federation decided to allow Slaney to compete, Gyulai said: "I don't believe any member of the IAAF can ignore the actions of the IAAF. There would be outrage."
Even if the U.S. federation clears Slaney, the IAAF would take the case to arbitration between the two federations, Gyulai said.

Farmer-Patrick, denied entry into the U.S. championships on Monday, was pursuing ways Tuesday to enter the meeting. Flenoy has a U.S. Olympic Committee arbitration hearing scheduled for Wednesday. If successful, he would be permitted to run.

Both a court hearing and arbitration remain options for Slaney. But her husband said, "I can't imagine Mary wanting to seek a court order or go to arbitration. So what ... (if she wins a court order or arbitration) she runs and wins. Then so what. She would not be allowed to compete in the world championships."

Slaney's attorney, Jim Coleman, accused USA Track and Field of not protecting her rights and said the organisation "would be held accountable" under the U.S. Amateur Sports Act and the U.S. Olympic Committee's constitution. He would not specify what action he planned to take.
